lessons.title: Types of animal fibre
lessons.html:
What is animal fibre?

Animal fibre is the hair or wool that grows on animals. It is cut off and sold to make clothes, blankets and carpets. South Africa is famous for its wool and mohair.

Main fibres

  • Wool: from sheep such as Merino and Dohne Merino. Fine, soft and crimpy.
  • Mohair: from Angora goats. Long, shiny and strong.
  • Cashmere: the soft undercoat of some goats.
  • Coarse hair: from some sheep breeds and other animals. Worth less.

Why sorting is important

Buyers pay more for clean, even fibre. If good wool is mixed with dirty, short or coloured fibre, the whole bale loses value. Sorting means putting fibre of the same kind and quality together.

Words you will hear

  • Fleece: all the wool from one sheep, in one piece.
  • Bellies: wool from the belly. Shorter and often dirty.
  • Pieces: wool from the edges of the fleece.
  • Locks: short bits that fall on the floor.
  • Crutchings: wool from around the tail and back legs. Often has dung.
  • Bale: a big pack of pressed wool or mohair for selling.

Each kind is kept apart in its own bin or bale.

lessons.title: Sorting fibre on the table
lessons.html:
Steps at the wool table

  1. The picker-up gathers the fleece off the shearing board and throws it out flat on the wool table, outside down.
  2. Take off the dirty edges, short bits and stained wool. This is called skirting. Put these pieces in the right bin.
  3. Look at the fleece. Check length, how fine it is, colour and how clean it is.
  4. The classer decides which class the fleece goes into. Do what the classer tells you.
  5. Roll the fleece and put it in the right bin.

What to take out

  • Dung and urine-stained wool.
  • Black, brown or coloured fibres. Even a few coloured fibres spoil white wool.
  • Grass seeds, burrs and sticks (vegetable matter).
  • Paint or marking crayon that will not wash out.
  • Wet wool. Wet wool can rot and catch fire in the bale.

Never put these in the bale

  • Plastic, string from feed bags, or polypropylene. Even small pieces spoil cloth in the factory.
  • Stones, sand or rubbish.
  • Fibre from different animals mixed together, such as wool and mohair.

Keep the floor and table clean. Sweep often and put sweepings in their own bin.

lessons.title: Packing, marking and working safely
lessons.html:
Packing the bale

  • Use only approved wool packs, not plastic feed bags.
  • Put only one class of fibre in each bale.
  • Press the bale to the right weight. Do not overfill.
  • Close the bale with the right fasteners.

Marking the bale

Each bale must be marked clearly with the farm brand, the class of fibre and the bale number. Use the stencil and marking ink the farm gives you. Write the details in the bale book. Wrong marking makes buyers lose trust and the farmer loses money.

Storing bales

  • Keep bales dry and off the ground, on pallets.
  • Keep them away from fuel, chemicals and fire.
  • Lock the store. Wool can be stolen.

Working safely

  • The wool press can crush hands. Only trained workers may use it. Keep your hands out when the press moves.
  • Lift bales with help or with a trolley. Bend your knees and keep your back straight.
  • Keep walkways clear so nobody trips.
  • No smoking in the shed. Wool burns.
  • Wash your hands before eating. Wool can carry dirt and germs.

Key points

  • Clean, even fibre gets a better price.
  • Skirt off dirty, stained and short wool and keep each kind in its own bin.
  • Never let plastic, string, coloured fibre or wet wool into the bale.
  • One class per bale, marked clearly and written in the bale book.
  • Keep hands out of the press and lift bales safely.
